beats.text: So what if, for one second, the ground under you stopped, and everything else didn't?

beats.text: First, the speed. Earth turns once every 23.93 hours relative to the stars. That's the sidereal day, about four minutes shorter than the 24-hour day on your clock, because Earth is also circling the Sun.

beats.text: Divide the distance around the equator by that time, and you get about 465 meters per second. That's roughly 1,670 kilometers per hour, faster than the speed of sound.
beats.template_text: Divide the distance around the equator by that time, and you get about {{v_eq_ms}} meters per second. That's roughly {{v_eq_kmh}} kilometers per hour, faster than the speed of sound.
beats.spoken: Divide the distance around the equator by that time, and you get about four hundred and sixty-five meters per second. That's roughly one thousand six hundred and seventy kilometers per hour, faster than the speed of sound.

beats.text: But not everyone moves that fast. The farther you are from the equator, the smaller the circle you trace every day.

beats.spoken: But not everyone moves that fast. The farther you are from the equator, the smaller the circle you trace every day.

beats.text: In Singapore, you're doing about 465 meters per second. In Cairo, 403. New York, 353. London, 290. And at the North Pole, you're just turning in place.

beats.spoken: In Singapore, you're doing about four hundred and sixty-five meters per second. In Cairo, four hundred and three. New York, three hundred and fifty-three. London, two hundred and ninety. And at the North Pole, you're just turning in place.

beats.text: We never feel any of this, because the ground, the air, the oceans and you are all moving together, at a steady speed. Motion you share with everything around you is motion you can't feel.

beats.text: Let's start the clock. At time zero, the ground stops. Say you're standing on the equator. From the ground's point of view, you're suddenly hurtling east at 465 meters per second.

beats.text: Can friction save you? Rubber on dry concrete can slow you down at about 6.9 meters per second squared. Over the whole second, that takes off just 7 meters per second. You'd still be going 458.

beats.text: If nothing were in your way, you'd tumble almost half a kilometer in that one second.

beats.text: But on a planet covered in walls, trees and cars, something is always in your way. So how hard is that hit?

beats.text: Here's another way to feel that number. Hitting a wall at that speed is like falling from a height of 11 kilometers, with no air to slow you down. That's higher than Mount Everest.

beats.text: Now, buildings. Unlike you, they're anchored to the rock. So when the rock stops, their foundations stop with it, instantly.

beats.text: The upper floors don't know that yet. The news travels up the structure as a shear wave, a kind of sound wave in steel, moving at about 3,200 meters per second.

beats.text: The stress that wave carries is density, times wave speed, times the sudden change in velocity. For steel, that's about 12 gigapascals.

beats.text: Common structural steel starts to give way in shear at around 140 megapascals. Our stress wave is about 80 times that. Structures bolted to the ground just aren't built for a jolt like this.

beats.text: And yet, as bad as all that is, it isn't the biggest problem. The biggest problem is the thing you can't see.

beats.text: The atmosphere isn't bolted to anything. When the ground stops, the air keeps going. At the equator, that's a wind of 465 meters per second, blowing from west to east.

beats.text: At sea level, sound travels at about 340 meters per second. So at the equator, this wind is Mach 1.37. It stays supersonic everywhere within about 43 degrees of the equator. That's two-thirds of Earth's surface, all at once.

beats.text: Anything standing in its way gets pushed with at least half the air density times the wind speed squared. That's 132 kilopascals, about 14 tonnes of force on every square meter of wall.

beats.text: For comparison, a Category 5 hurricane starts at 252 kilometers per hour. That push grows with the square of the speed, so our wind pushes about 44 times harder than the minimum Category 5 wind.

beats.text: Across that zone, every building, tree and hill would grow its own shock wave. Picture a sonic boom, but instead of one passing jet, it comes from every obstacle at the same moment.

metadata.hook: Right now Earth's spin carries you at up to 1,670 km/h (465 m/s). What if, for one second, the ground stopped and nothing else did?
metadata.summary: We run the scenario through real physics and show every calculation on screen: the supersonic wind, the shear wave through every building, water hammer on the coasts, ocean-wide tsunamis, the restart, and the one permanent change (Earth ends up exactly one second late).
key_numbers: Wind if the ground stops: Mach 1.37, ram pressure ≥ 132 kPa (≈ 44× a minimum Cat-5 wind)
Your kinetic energy at the equator (70 kg): 7.6 MJ ≈ 1.8 kg TNT ≈ the energy of a 11 km fall
Shear wave in steel: τ = ρ c Δv ≈ 12 GPa ≈ 80× shear yield
Water hammer: Δp = ρ c Δv ≈ 720 MPa, more than 6× the Challenger Deep pressure
Tsunami speed √(g·d) at 3.7 km depth: 684 km/h
metadata.assumptions: Assumptions: the solid Earth stops instantly, holds for exactly 1 s, then resumes. Wave heights are not estimated (they need coastline-resolving simulations).
